newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Bear Stearns sees CVRD sold despite delays.
newsitem.headline: Bear Stearns sees CVRD sold despite delays.

text.p: Bear Stearns said it is sure Brazilian state miner Cia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) eventually will be sold despite recent delays stemming from a spate of legal challenges.

"Although the privatization auction for CVRD originally scheduled for April 29 has been at least temporarily blocked by court order, we believe that the privatization process will ultimately be concluded," the brokerage said in a report.

Bear Stearns also said that, no matter which consortium wins the bidding, CVRD will retain its stakes in local steel firms Cia Siderurgica de Tubarao (CST), California Steel Industries (CSI) and Acominas.

CVRD, which directly and indirectly participated in 75 percent of Brazil's total steel output last year, or 19 million tonnes, also owns stakes in Usiminas, Cia Siderurgica Nacional (CSN), Siderar and Cosipa.
"Given CVRD's portfolio of sizeable holdings, its winning bidder will be able to claim seats on the boards of some of its main competitors," the brokerage said.
As a result, Brazil's anti-trust commission CADE may have to step in to "preclude competitors from having undue influence on the operations of their rivals," it added.

Bear Stearns also said the privatization should lead to consolidation among Brazil's pulp and paper producers. CVRD owns 45 percent of Bahia Sul, 51.5 percent of Cenibra, 42.5 percent of Celmar and 99.9 percent of FRD.
The Votorantim group, which leads the consortium favored to win the bidding, owns major pulp producer Votorantim Celulose e Papel SA.
Other members of the consortium -- Anglo-American Corp of South Africa and Banco Safra -- each own 28 percent of pulp giant Aracruz Celulose e Papel SA, it added.
The second consortium, led by CSN, includes as a member paper firm Cia Suzano de Celulose e Papel SA, which owns 55 percent of Bahia Sul.

In the aluminum sector, CVRD's other main activity, the winning bidder will control extraction of bauxite in Brazil, but competition is likely to continue in the conversion of bauxite into alumina and further processing of alumina into aluminum.
